title: Personal finance
description: The few principles that do most of the work in saving, borrowing and investing.

ideas.title: Compound interest
ideas.summary: Money that earns interest on its interest grows faster each year, so starting early matters a great deal.

items.q: What is compound interest?
items.a: Interest earned on both the original amount and the interest already added to it

items.q: What is the rule of 72?
items.a: Divide 72 by the annual percentage growth rate (6 for 6%) to estimate the years needed to double

items.q: By the rule of 72, about how long does money take to double at 6% a year?
items.a: About 12 years

items.q: By the rule of 72, what annual return doubles your money in about 9 years?
items.a: About 8%

items.q: Why does starting to save ten years earlier make such a large difference to the final sum?
items.a: The early money compounds for longer, and most compound growth comes in the later years

ideas.title: APR and APY
ideas.summary: APR states a yearly rate without compounding; APY includes compounding and shows what you really earn or pay.

items.q: What does APR stand for?
items.a: Annual percentage rate

items.q: What does APY stand for, and what does it include that APR does not?
items.a: Annual percentage yield; it includes the effect of compounding

items.q: A credit card charges 24% APR. Roughly what rate is that per month?
items.a: About 2% per month

items.q: Which figure should you compare when choosing between savings accounts, and why?
items.a: The APY, because it includes compounding and shows what you will actually earn

ideas.title: The emergency fund
ideas.summary: A cash reserve of a few months' expenses lets you absorb a shock without borrowing or selling investments.

items.q: How many months of essential expenses is an emergency fund commonly meant to cover?
items.a: Three to six months

items.q: Where is an emergency fund best kept?
items.a: Somewhere safe and easy to reach, such as a savings account, not in stocks

items.q: What is an emergency fund for?
items.a: Unexpected, necessary costs such as a lost job, a medical bill or an urgent repair

items.q: In finance, what does liquidity mean?
items.a: How quickly and cheaply something can be turned into cash

ideas.title: Index funds and diversification
ideas.summary: An index fund tracks a chosen index; broad-market funds can spread exposure across many holdings.

items.q: What is an index fund?
items.a: A fund that holds the securities in a market index, aiming to match its return, not beat it

items.q: In investing, what is diversification?
items.a: Spreading investments across holdings and asset types to reduce concentration risk; it cannot eliminate all risk

items.q: What is a fund's expense ratio?
items.a: The yearly fee, as a percentage of the money you have invested in the fund

items.q: What is the difference between a stock and a bond?
items.a: A stock is a share of ownership in a company; a bond is a loan to a company or government

items.q: What is dollar-cost averaging?
items.a: Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals, whatever the price

ideas.title: Debt
ideas.summary: Interest on debt compounds against you, so high-rate debt is usually the first thing to clear.

items.q: With fixed rates and no prepayment penalties, after all minimum payments, which debt should receive extra payments to minimize interest?
items.a: The one with the highest interest rate (the avalanche method)

items.q: What is the debt snowball method?
items.a: Paying off the smallest balance first, to build momentum, while paying the minimum on the rest

items.q: Why is paying only the minimum on a credit card costly?
items.a: The balance is repaid slowly, so interest can accrue for much longer than if you paid more each month

ideas.title: Inflation and real return
ideas.summary: Inflation erodes what money buys, so what counts is the return you earn above it.

items.q: What is inflation?
items.a: A general rise in prices over time, which reduces what each unit of money can buy

items.q: What is the real return on an investment?
items.a: The inflation-adjusted return: (1 + nominal return) / (1 + inflation rate) - 1; subtraction is an approximation

items.q: If an investment returns 7% in a year when inflation is 3%, roughly what is the real return?
items.a: About 4%
